titre: Fallingwater Has Been Sagging Since the Day Its Scaffolding Was Removed
accroche: The very day the scaffolding comes off its second-floor terrace, a crack already appears in Frank Lloyd Wright's masterpiece.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1936, Frank Lloyd Wright begins construction of Fallingwater, the house he designed for the Kaufmann family above a waterfall in Pennsylvania, holding its concrete terraces up by cantilever directly over the water; the Kaufmanns will not move in until November 1937. As soon as the scaffolding is removed from the second-floor terrace, a crack is said to have appeared, according to an anecdote that has remained famous among the engineers who have worked on the building since: one of them is said to have exclaimed that he had forgotten to put in the negative reinforcement, the steel bars meant to prevent precisely this kind of cracking.

## A Reinforcement Added in Secret

In August 1936, while the first-level terrace is being poured, Kaufmann asks the engineering firm Metzger-Richardson to draw up plans to strengthen the reinforcement. Wright rejects these plans: he is convinced that this additional steel, far from strengthening the terraces, would overload them. The site contractor pours, in secret, more reinforcing steel into the concrete than Wright's plans called for.

This precaution is not enough. As early as 1955, the Kaufmanns themselves document a sag in the terraces of about ten centimeters from their original position. In 1994, a University of Virginia student's thesis establishes that the sag now exceeds seventeen centimeters in places. The firm Robert Silman Associates is then commissioned for a full study, which results in a five-volume report: the concrete and steel of the terraces, it concludes, are overloaded because of design errors in the original reinforcement, to the point of no longer fulfilling their load-bearing function.

Between 2001 and 2002, high-strength steel cables are anchored in the concrete piers beneath the house, then fixed to three of the four main beams of the living room and put under tension, stopping the sag without touching the building's appearance. The deformation already accumulated, however, remains: correcting it would have reopened cracks that a sag frozen for decades had ended up stabilizing.

## What This Shifts

The most photographed building in 20th-century architecture has therefore never stood as Wright drew it: it survived only thanks to the reinforcing steel added against his advice during construction, then the cables tensioned sixty-five years later by the engineers who succeeded him. What history remembers as a pure architectural gesture, the house suspended above its waterfall, actually rested on a technical disagreement that Wright lost without ever admitting it.

quiz.question: According to the Robert Silman Associates report, why have Fallingwater's terraces gradually sagged since 1936?
choix: Design errors in the original reinforcement overloaded the concrete and steel of the cantilevers, which no longer fulfilled their load-bearing role
The waterfall beneath the house slowly eroded the stone foundations on which the terraces rest
A fire in 1943 had seriously weakened the steel framework without the damage being repaired at the time
Pennsylvania's humid climate rusted the reinforcing bars to the point of destroying all their strength
quiz.explication: The five-volume Robert Silman Associates report, which led to the 2001-2002 strengthening campaign, identified design errors in the cantilevers' original reinforcement, insufficient for the loads they were to carry. Neither erosion, nor a fire, nor corrosion of the bars alone explains the sag measured since the 1950s.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Kaufmann ask the firm Metzger-Richardson for in August 1936, and how does Wright react?
choix: An additional soil study ahead of construction, which Wright accepts without reservation
Plans to strengthen the reinforcement, which Wright rejects, judging the steel unnecessary
A complete change of material, replacing reinforced concrete with bare steel
Moving the house to a spot less exposed to the neighboring waterfall
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Kaufmann asks for plans to strengthen the reinforcement while the terrace is being poured; Wright rejects them, convinced that the additional steel would overload the terraces rather than strengthen them.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the site contractor do despite Wright's rejection of the strengthening plans?
choix: He pours, in secret, more reinforcing steel into the concrete than Wright's plans called for
He immediately informs the Kaufmanns of the disagreement and halts construction
He follows Wright's plans to the letter, adding no reinforcement at all
He replaces the planned concrete entirely with a lighter material
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The contractor pours, in secret, more reinforcing steel than Wright had planned, a precaution that will nonetheless not be enough to prevent the sag measured as early as 1955.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What puts an end to the sagging of Fallingwater's terraces between 2001 and 2002?
choix: Completely replacing the concrete terraces with a new steel structure
Adding an extra support pier directly in the waterfall's bed
Reducing the house's weight by removing its original furniture
Steel cables anchored in the piers and tensioned, fixed to three of the living room's four beams
quiz_supplementaire.explication: High-strength steel cables are anchored in the concrete piers, fixed to three of the living room's four main beams and put under tension, stopping the sag without touching the building's appearance.
